strengths: Introduces Long-RVOS, a large-scale long-term RVOS benchmark with 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 seconds, 24,689 text descriptions, 6,703 objects, and 163 object classes, addressing the short-video limitation of existing RVOS datasets.

Provides three description types (static, dynamic, hybrid) for fine-grained evaluation and reports balanced description distributions, helping avoid bias toward static attributes such as color or position.
Proposes two new evaluation metrics, tIoU and vIoU, to measure temporal and spatiotemporal consistency beyond per-frame J&F, exposing failures caused by missing or spurious masks in long videos.

Benchmarks six state-of-the-art RVOS methods under consistent training settings and demonstrates substantial performance drops on Long-RVOS; SAM2 oracle analysis further quantifies the long-term tracking challenge.

Proposes ReferMo, a motion-enhanced local-to-global baseline that achieves the best overall J&F (51.3) and vIoU (42.6) among compared methods, with ablations showing clear benefits from motion information and keyframe supervision.
The paper is well written, with clear figures, tables, annotation protocol, implementation details, and dataset statistics that make the benchmark accessible and reproducible.
weaknesses: Mask annotations are generated by SAM2 propagated from sparse bounding boxes and then human-corrected, rather than fully manual pixel-level annotation; no quantitative mask quality or inter-annotator agreement is reported, so annotation noise could affect benchmark reliability.

The proposed vIoU is not a true spatiotemporal volume IoU; it averages per-frame J over frames where both masks are non-empty and divides by the union of frame indices, which may not faithfully measure volumetric segmentation overlap.

ReferMo is largely an integration of existing components (MPEG-4 motion vectors, keyframe sampling, ReferDINO-style object decoding, and SAM2 tracking), so architectural novelty is moderate; gains over the strongest baseline, ReferDINO, are modest in overall J&F (+2.6) and tIoU is slightly lower.

Evaluation is limited to Long-RVOS with six compared methods; there is no cross-dataset generalization experiment (e.g., to MeViS or LVOS) and no comparison to long-video VOS methods without text, so robustness of conclusions is somewhat narrow.

The dataset is built by filtering existing video datasets (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), which may inherit source-domain biases; the inferred frame rate from mean frames and duration appears to be about 6 fps, potentially missing fine-grained motion.

Text annotations were collected from 20 college students and validated by three experts, but no detailed annotation-quality metrics, agreement statistics, or user study are provided to substantiate the claimed diversity and authenticity.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear limitation of existing RVOS benchmarks: most prior datasets are short and contain mostly visible targets, while Long-RVOS provides 2,193 videos with a mean duration of 60.3 seconds, 2.1M masks, 6,703 objects, 163 object classes, and 24,689 text descriptions, substantially improving scale and duration over prior RVOS benchmarks.

The benchmark includes explicit annotation of static, dynamic, and hybrid description types, enabling fine-grained evaluation of model capabilities beyond overall average performance. This is a useful diagnostic contribution for the RVOS community.

The introduced tIoU and vIoU metrics extend frame-wise J&F evaluation toward temporal and spatiotemporal consistency, which is important for long-video RVOS where targets may disappear, reappear, and undergo occlusion.

The paper benchmarks six recent RVOS methods under a common training protocol and includes an oracle SAM2 analysis, convincingly showing that current approaches struggle on long-term RVOS and that a large gap remains relative to short-video benchmarks.

The proposed ReferMo baseline integrates motion vectors and a local-to-global architecture, and ablation studies show that motion information improves keyframe segmentation and that performance saturates with a modest number of motion frames.
The paper is generally well organized, with informative figures and tables that clearly communicate dataset statistics, benchmark results, and ablation findings.
weaknesses: Mask annotation quality is not quantitatively validated. The masks are largely generated by SAM2 from sparse source bounding boxes, with an iterative check-correct workflow, but the paper reports no inter-annotator agreement, human verification accuracy, or failure-rate analysis. For a benchmark paper, this is a significant concern because SAM2 errors could bias evaluation.

The dataset is constructed by repurposing existing long-video datasets such as TAO, VidOR, and Ego-Exo4D rather than collecting new videos. This may introduce source-domain biases, and the average duration of about 60 seconds, while longer than prior RVOS benchmarks, is still far from truly long-form real-world videos. The test set is also relatively small at 225 videos.

The new metrics are adapted from spatiotemporal video grounding but are not fully robust on their own. tIoU considers only whether predicted and ground-truth masks are non-empty, so a model could match temporal presence intervals while segmenting the wrong object, while vIoU averages J only over frames where both masks are non-empty and can under-penalize false-positive masks on absent frames.

ReferMo's keyframe-only improvement over ReferDINO without SAM2 is modest, about 0.5% J&F, while its final benchmark gains rely heavily on SAM2 for mask propagation on non-keyframes. This makes the architectural contribution of ReferMo somewhat unclear and suggests that the reported gains may be partly attributable to the tracker rather than the proposed motion-aware reasoning.

The method comparison may be confounded by differing backbones, training schedules, and use of SAM/SAM2. Although the paper separates methods with and without SAM/SAM2, the experimental protocol is not fully controlled, and no cross-dataset generalization or detailed failure-case analysis is provided.

Reproducibility is only partially established: implementation details and compute resources are given, but the paper does not clearly state public release of annotations, code, or evaluation server, and the annotation pipeline lacks sufficient quantitative validation for independent reproduction.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap: existing RVOS benchmarks (Ref-DAVIS17, Ref-YouTube-VOS, MeViS, A2D-Sentences) are limited to short clips (a few seconds) with the target visible in most frames, whereas Long-RVOS targets minute-level videos (avg 60.3s, 2,193 videos, 36.7h) with occlusion, disappearance-reappearance, and shot changes.

The benchmark is large and diverse: 24,689 text descriptions, 2.1M masks, 163 object classes, and videos integrated from several long-video sources (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D), substantially exceeding prior RVOS datasets in scale and duration.

Introduces two temporal evaluation metrics (tIoU and vIoU) that complement the frame-wise J&F, and categorizes descriptions into static/dynamic/hybrid types, which is a reasonable step toward more comprehensive evaluation of temporal consistency and of model bias.

The benchmarking of six recent RVOS methods is informative, and the finding that SAM2-based pipelines degrade significantly on long videos (e.g., SAMWISE ~36 J&F) is a useful, non-obvious observation for the community.

ReferMo is a sensible engineering baseline: exploiting MPEG-4 motion vectors (cheap to extract during decoding) and supervising only keyframes keeps training cost bounded (24h on 8×A6000) while still improving over baselines; the ablation on motion length is a clean control.
The paper is clearly written and well-organized, with informative figures (duration comparison, annotation examples, dataset statistics) and a readable method description.
weaknesses: Ground-truth mask quality is a foundational concern for a benchmark paper and is not quantitatively validated. Masks are produced by SAM2 from sparse bounding boxes provided by source datasets, then 'corrected' by nine annotators in a check-correct loop. No human-agreement study, no comparison against a manually annotated subset, and no per-mask quality statistics are reported, so the reliability of the 2.1M 'ground-truth' masks—and therefore of every number in Tables 2–3—remains unverified. This is not a mere presentation gap; if the masks drift or are biased toward SAM2 outputs, the benchmark may reward SAM2-consistent behavior rather than correct referring segmentation.

The central 'significant improvement' claim is not apples-to-apples. ReferMo uses SAM2 at inference for mask propagation on non-keyframes, while the strongest comparison point (ReferDINO, 48.7 J&F overall) is listed under 'Without SAM/SAM2.' The overall gap is only ~2.6 J&F (51.3 vs 48.7), and a substantial portion plausibly comes from SAM2's tracking rather than from the proposed motion/local-to-global design. The claim would be much stronger if compared against SAM2-equipped baselines under identical inference budgets.

The new temporal-consistency metric does not support the stated conclusion: on tIoU, ReferMo (71.2) is worse than ReferDINO (71.7), which the authors acknowledge but then still frame as an overall temporal-consistency improvement. Additionally, tIoU is a coarse set-overlap metric that ignores temporal ordering (predicting the right number of non-empty frames at the wrong times scores highly), and the observed range across methods (67–71) is narrow, limiting its discriminative value.

Technical novelty of ReferMo is limited. Motion-vector-based compression and keyframe+motion decomposition are directly borrowed from Video-LaVIT, and the local-perception-to-global-interaction design closely follows prior object-centric RVOS pipelines (e.g., ReferDINO's Hungarian alignment and cross-clip attention). The genuinely novel component—the gated image-motion fusion—is a standard low-rank + channel-gate residual block.

The paper reports no variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing for any of the main comparisons, so the small margins (e.g., 51.3 vs 48.7, or 49.6 vs 49.1 on keyframes) cannot be distinguished from run-to-run noise.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the abstract asserts ReferMo 'achieves significant improvements over current methods,' and the introduction asserts that current metrics 'cannot adequately reflect temporal consistency,' yet the benchmark itself shows tIoU is high and relatively uniform across methods, undercutting the motivating argument for the metric.

The three description types (static/dynamic/hybrid) are presented as a key contribution, but the resulting finding—models are biased toward static attributes and perform worst on dynamic descriptions—is largely expected from the RVOS literature, and no analysis is provided to show that the taxonomy enables any new diagnostic capability beyond what MeViS's motion-expression split already provides.

strengths: Addresses an important gap: existing RVOS benchmarks are short and mostly contain salient objects, while Long-RVOS is the first minute-level large-scale RVOS benchmark with 2,193 videos averaging 60.3s, 2.1M masks, 6,703 objects, 163 classes, and 24,689 text descriptions (Table 1, Figs. 1 and 5).

Rich and well-designed annotation: introduces Static, Dynamic, and Hybrid description types with a balanced distribution (Table 2), multi-source video collection, and a check-correct mask annotation workflow involving multiple annotators and expert validation.
Proposes tIoU and vIoU to evaluate temporal and spatiotemporal consistency beyond frame-wise J&F (Eqs. 1-2), revealing that current models have weak temporal consistency despite high J&F scores.

Extensive benchmark: evaluates 7 recent RVOS methods under a controlled training setting, with oracle analysis showing that even SAM2 with ground-truth first-frame prompts drops from 77-80 J&F on MeViS to 54-56 J&F on Long-RVOS (Table 4a), convincingly demonstrating long-video difficulty.

The ReferMo baseline is simple, efficient, and effective: it integrates motion features into keyframe clips, performs local-to-global interaction, trains only on keyframe annotations, and uses SAM2 for propagation, achieving 52.9 J&F / 73.6 tIoU / 45.2 vIoU at 52.5 FPS (Table 3).

Thorough ablations and analyses: video decomposition, mask propagation methods, global interaction, image-motion gating, occlusion robustness, description length, and event complexity are all studied (Tables 4-6, 10-12), with qualitative comparisons in Fig. 8.
The paper is clearly organized, well illustrated, and discusses limitations and future work, making the benchmark accessible and useful for the community.
weaknesses: Mask annotations are model-assisted rather than fully manually annotated: source datasets provide sparse bounding boxes, and SAM2 is used to generate masks with first-frame prompts, followed by human refinement. This may inherit SAM2 drift or systematic errors in long videos with occlusion and disappearance-reappearance, potentially affecting ground-truth reliability.

The new metrics have conceptual ambiguities: tIoU is essentially a frame-presence set IoU, not temporal overlap or ordering, and vIoU as defined in Eq. 2 is an average frame IoU over intersection presence frames divided by the union presence count, not a true spatiotemporal volume IoU. Their naming and interpretation as temporal/spatiotemporal consistency are not rigorously validated.

Comparison scope is limited: all models are trained solely on Long-RVOS, while several SAM/SAM2-based methods rely on large external pretraining. The paper does not explore fine-tuning or external-data settings, so absolute practical SOTA conclusions remain unclear.

ReferMo is largely an integration of existing components (Swin backbone, motion vectors, ReferDINO-style object temporal enhancement, Hungarian matching, SAM2 propagation). Its gains over ReferDINO are moderate (e.g., +4.5 J&F overall, +0.1 tIoU on Static), and it depends on off-the-shelf SAM2 without end-to-end fine-tuning.

Dataset source reuse introduces potential bias and overlap concerns: Long-RVOS is built from existing video datasets (TAO, VidOR, Ego-Exo4D, Charades, LaSOT, AVA, etc.), and some videos may overlap with pretraining data of evaluated models. The distribution is human-centric (71.9% human) and lacks background stuff classes, as acknowledged.

Long-term absence is still limited: average object duration is 47.8s within 60.3s videos (~79% presence), and only 11.5% of videos contain long-term reappearance (LRA) (Table 8), so the benchmark may not stress long-term disappearance as strongly as its total duration suggests.

Reproducibility and release details are incomplete: the project page link is blank in the manuscript, code/dataset release is not explicitly stated, and annotation tools are only described in the supplement. This may hinder adoption and verification.

Evaluation breadth and statistical reporting are modest: only 7 methods are benchmarked, no variance or error bars are reported across runs, and FPS is estimated excluding video loading time, which may overstate practical efficiency.

strengths: The paper introduces Long-RVOS, a large-scale long-term RVOS benchmark with 2,193 videos, 36.7 hours, 60.3s average duration, 2.1M masks, 6,703 objects, 163 classes, and 24,689 text descriptions (Table 1). This is a substantial and timely resource: prior RVOS datasets focus on short clips (e.g., MeViS 13.2s), while Long-RVOS targets minute-level videos with occlusion, disappearance/reappearance, and shot changes.

Annotation design is thoughtful: three description types (Static, Dynamic, Hybrid) balance object attributes, motion, and spatiotemporal relations (Table 2, Fig. 2); masks are generated with SAM2 and refined via an iterative check-correct workflow, with expert validation.

It proposes tIoU and vIoU metrics to measure temporal consistency and spatiotemporal overlap, addressing the fact that frame-wise J&F alone can overestimate robustness in videos where the target is absent due to occlusion or out-of-view.

Extensive benchmarking: 7 SOTA methods compared under controlled training on Long-RVOS, plus fine-grained evaluation across description types, occlusion rates, event complexity, and description length (Tables 3,6,11,12; Fig. 3).

ReferMo baseline is simple but effective: MPEG-4 motion vectors, local-to-global architecture, and keyframe-only supervision with SAM2 propagation; it achieves best overall J&F (52.9), tIoU (73.6), vIoU (45.2) and 52.5 FPS, with ablations validating video decomposition, global interaction, motion/gating, and mask propagation (Tables 3,4,5,10).
Oracle analysis with SAM2 (54.3–56.6 J&F on Long-RVOS vs 77.3–80.6 on MeViS) convincingly demonstrates the long-video challenge and supports the need for the benchmark (Table 4a).
Reproducibility is supported by detailed implementation, hyperparameters, motion extraction, training/inference equations, and qualitative comparisons (Secs. 4,5; Supp. Secs. 7–11; Fig. 8).
Writing is clear and well-organized, with sufficient dataset statistics and visualizations to convey scope and difficulty.
weaknesses: vIoU is not a true volume IoU: it averages spatial IoU only on frames where both predicted and ground-truth masks are non-empty and normalizes by the union of non-empty frame-index sets. It ignores frames where one side is empty, so it can overstate spatial accuracy. The claim of 'spatiotemporal volume overlap' is technically inaccurate; tIoU partially compensates but vIoU should be redefined.

Mask quality is not quantitatively validated. Masks are propagated by SAM2 from sparse source bounding boxes and corrected manually, but the paper reports no human verification rate, inter-annotator agreement, or comparison against independent manual masks. For a benchmark, this is a notable reliability concern.

Text annotation quality is not quantified: no inter-annotator agreement, no measure of whether descriptions uniquely identify targets, and no evaluation of naturalness/diversity beyond word cloud. The 20-student annotation process may not capture real user query distribution.

Controlled training on Long-RVOS only, while fair for comparison, may disadvantage MLLM/SAM-based methods that normally rely on large-scale external pretraining. The paper's conclusion that current methods 'struggle severely' is valid for this setting, but absolute SOTA claims are limited.

The validation set is small (112 videos, 1,326 descriptions) compared with the test set (226 videos, 2,641 descriptions), and no split-bias or cross-source generalization analysis is provided. This could affect benchmark reliability and model selection.

ReferMo's inference relies on SAM2 for mask propagation, so its performance is bounded by SAM2. Oracle SAM2 with ground-truth prompts already achieves higher J&F (54.3–56.6) than ReferMo (52.9), indicating that the benchmark is not fully solved and that reported gains partly reflect better keyframe prompting/propagation rather than complete long-term reasoning.
The benchmark is human-centric (71.9% human instances) and excludes background stuff classes; while acknowledged, this limits generality for broader RVOS scenarios.

strengths: Addresses a real gap with a substantial resource: Long-RVOS provides 2,193 videos averaging 60.3 s (36.7 h total, 361.7 frames/video), 2.1 M masks, 6,703 objects and 24,689 descriptions. This is roughly a 4.5x increase in mean duration over MeViS (13.2 s) and a 5x increase in total annotated duration (Table 1), which genuinely extends RVOS toward minute-level videos with occlusion, out-of-view and disappearance-reappearance (Table 8: OV 61.0%, FOC 36.2%, LRA 11.5%).

The three description types (Static 35.03% / Dynamic 32.45% / Hybrid 32.52%, Table 2) are balanced and provide a controlled axis for probing attribute understanding vs. motion/spatiotemporal relations; this is a sensible design that most prior RVOS benchmarks do not offer.

The two proposed metrics target a genuine blind spot of frame-averaged J&F, namely that a model which never predicts absence is not penalized. The paper provides concrete evidence that the metrics disentangle presence prediction from segmentation quality: VideoLISA has tIoU 70.0 but J&F 14.0, whereas RGA3 has tIoU 60.0 and J&F 22.5 (Table 3).

The benchmark study is broad and reasonably systematic: 7 methods under one protocol, ablations on video decomposition (Table 4b), propagation model (Table 4c), gating (Table 10), global interaction (Table 5), plus robustness analyses by occlusion rate (Table 6), description length (Table 11) and event complexity (Table 12), and an oracle SAM2 study (Table 4a).

The claim that ReferMo's gains are not merely inherited from SAM2 is supported by Table 4c (ReferMo with XMem++ 50.4, Cutie 50.2, both well above the SAM2-based SAMWISE at 40.9 in Table 3), and the paper is transparent that SAM2 propagation contributes 2.5-2.7 J&F.
The paper is clearly written, well organized and honest about limitations (Section 12), which makes the contribution easy to assess.
weaknesses: Ground-truth masks are model-generated: SAM2 is run from sparse source-dataset boxes on a per-clip basis, then human-checked/corrected. No quantitative annotation-quality evidence is reported at all (no fraction of masks corrected, no inter-annotator agreement, no comparison against independently human-annotated masks, no boundary-accuracy measure). For a benchmark whose purpose is to rank RVOS models, this is a material omission, not a presentation detail.

Circularity/anchoring risk: the benchmark is bootstrapped from SAM2 and is then used to evaluate SAM2-based methods. The paper itself shows SAM2 propagation yields 2.5-2.7 J&F (Table 4c), and human 'check-correct' of SAM2 output is prone to accepting SAM2-like masks. Table 1 lists 'Masks' for Long-RVOS next to human-annotated competitors without disclosing that Long-RVOS masks are model-generated; this is potentially misleading in the paper's central comparison table.

The oracle analysis (Table 4a: 54.3-55.6 J&F on Long-RVOS vs. 77.3-80.6 on MeViS) is used as the key evidence that 'long-term' is the challenge. Because masks are re-prompted with SAM2 at each clip start, part of this gap can come from annotation discontinuities at clip boundaries rather than model drift. No control (e.g., re-prompting SAM2 at every clip start) is provided to separate the two explanations.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified in a way that directly affects the headline numbers: it is never stated how J and F are defined when the GT mask is empty and when the prediction is empty. Given that absent-object frames are pervasive in this dataset (OV 61.0%, FOC 36.2%), different conventions would shift the reported J&F (38-53 in Table 3) substantially. This is a reproducibility problem for the main results table.

vIoU is named 'volume IoU' but is defined as (1/|T_u|) * sum_{t in T_i} J_t, which is not a volumetric IoU (sum |intersection| / sum |union|) but a presence-weighted mean per-frame IoU. The naming/definition mismatch should be corrected or explicitly justified.

tIoU is simply the IoU of the binary non-empty-mask index sets; it captures presence prediction only and says nothing about temporal consistency of the segmentation itself (boundary stability, identity switches). The paper repeatedly describes it as a temporal-consistency metric without any experiment linking it to identity-switch or stability behavior.

Technical novelty of ReferMo is modest: MPEG-4 motion vectors (borrowed from Video-LaViT), keyframe + motion clip decomposition, factorized spatial/temporal attention, gated image-motion fusion, dual cross-attention, object-level temporal interaction (essentially ReferDINO's OTE) and SAM2 propagation. The paper itself concedes 'despite simplicity', and the contribution reads mainly as a well-executed integration of existing components.

The comparison protocol retrains every baseline solely on Long-RVOS with no image-segmentation pretraining. Although this follows MeViS's convention, the MLLM-based methods (VideoLISA 14.0, GLUS 25.7, RGA3 22.5) are far outside their intended training regime, so the conclusion that 'SAM-based methods significantly struggle in Long-RVOS' and the attribution of their short-benchmark success to SAM2's tracker are confounded by training data/regime. Reporting the same baselines on their original benchmarks under an identical retraining budget would isolate the long-video effect.

Claim-evidence mismatch: the abstract and Figure 2 assert coverage of 'shot changing', but the attribute list in Tables 7/8 (POC, FOC, OV, LRA, VC, ARC, SV, CM, MB) contains no shot-change attribute, so this claimed coverage is never quantified.

A 'comprehensive benchmark' paper should stratify model performance by the video attributes it tabulates. Table 8 attributes (POC/FOC/OV/LRA/VC/ARC/SV/CM/MB) are never used to break down results; there is no human upper bound, no error taxonomy, and the validation set (112 videos / 1,326 descriptions) is small. Test results (226 videos) are self-reported with no held-out server, which allows tuning on the test split by the authors' own method.

Reproducibility gaps beyond the metrics: the keyframe-selection criterion from MPEG-4 is not concretely specified; Eq. (6) is block matching with an unspecified search range and is described inconsistently as 'MPEG-4 motion vectors'; the training setting ('3-frame motion vectors') contradicts the stated 'up to 11 subsequent frames'; the occlusion-rate definition used in Table 6 is never given; and the dataset release plan, licensing, derived-data redistribution constraints for Ego-Exo4D/TAO/VidOR, and annotator compensation are not discussed.

Object distribution is heavily human-centric (71.9% human, 12.7% animal, 15.4% instrument; Fig. 4) and long-tailed (Fig. 3), while background stuff classes are excluded. The 'most diverse object classes' claim (163) is technically true but overstates practical diversity.
